name: Gori Temple
significance: A Shvetambara Jain temple of marble in the Nagarparkar area of Sindh, dedicated to Parshvanatha and holding twenty-four small cells for the twenty-four Tirthankaras. Its design is compared to the Jain temples of Mount Abu, and it survives as one of the most important Jain monuments left in Pakistan.
story: Local tradition credits the temple to a Jain devotee named Gorichom, from whom its name is said to derive.

name: Akkana Basadi
significance: A Hoysala-period Jain basadi at Shravanabelagola, built in 1181 during the reign of Veera Ballala II by Achiyakka (Achala Devi), wife of the minister Chandramouli. It is among the best preserved of the town's smaller basadis and is dedicated to Parshvanatha.

name: Bajramath Temple, Gyaraspur
significance: A ninth-century temple at Gyaraspur with three sanctums in a row, now enshrining Jain Tirthankara images and protected by the Archaeological Survey of India. Its carving is a well-known example of post-Gupta workmanship under Pratihara patronage.

name: Kere Basadi
significance: A Jain basadi standing on an island in the middle of a lake at Varanga, reached by boat, with four entrances facing the images of Parshvanatha, Neminatha, Shantinatha and Anantanatha. Inscriptions record land grants from the Vijayanagara ruler Deva Raya II in 1424 and later donors in the sixteenth century.
story: Devotees hold that a flower falling from the right side of the image is a sign of the Tirthankara's blessing.

name: Shantinath Jain Teerth
significance: A modern Digambara Jain pilgrimage temple near Indapur, opened in 2011 and built to a South Indian design. Its principal image is a 27-foot granite figure of Munisuvrata weighing about thirty tons, carved over two years from stone quarried near Bengaluru; the gilded facade has earned it the local name of the Golden Temple.

name: Shantinatha Temple, Ramtek
significance: A Digambara Jain temple at Ramtek dated to the eleventh or twelfth century and built of yellow sandstone in the northern Indian manner. Further shrines were added to the complex in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries by an official of the Bhonsle court at Nagpur, and it has since hosted several chaturmas retreats of Acharya Vidyasagar.

name: Jain Temples, Pavagadh
significance: A group of Jain temples on Pavagadh Hill, mostly of the thirteenth century and associated with Vastupala, minister of the Vaghela rulers. Originally Shvetambara foundations, they later passed to the Digambara community, and the hill's Jain associations are traced back in tradition to an image installed by King Samprati.
story: The Achalgacch order is said to have begun here when the demi-goddess Mahakali appeared before Acharya Aryarakshitsuri as he climbed the hill to undertake sallekhana and asked him not to proceed.

name: Neminath Jain Temple, Girnar
significance: The principal and largest of the Jain temples on Girnar hill, dedicated to Neminatha, whose oldest surviving portion was raised about 1129 CE by Sajjana, the Chaulukya governor of Saurashtra. It anchors one of the most important Jain pilgrimage hills in western India.
story: A layman named Ratnasar is said to have bathed an ancient clay image until it dissolved, and after a fast of twenty-one days to have received a stone image of Neminatha from the demi-goddess Ambika, consecrated in Vikram Samvat 980.

name: Digambara Jain Temple, Khandagiri
style: Kalinga, pidha deul with vimana and jagamohana
significance: The living Digambara Jain temple on the summit of Khandagiri hill above the ancient Jain caves at Bhubaneswar, its present structure built in the first quarter of the nineteenth century in Kalinga style. The main shrine holds Parshvanatha along with images of Mahavira and other Tirthankaras.
story: Local legend attributes the temple to the Kalinga king Kharavela of the first century BCE, an attribution its architecture does not support.

name: Sarnath Jain Tirth
significance: A Jain temple at Sarnath built in 1824, revered by both Digambaras and Shvetambaras, holding a large image of Shreyansanatha together with his footprint impressions. It marks the site associated with four of that Tirthankara's five kalyanakas.
story: Singhpuri beside Sarnath is held to be the ancient Simhapuri where Shreyansanatha was conceived, born, renounced the world and attained omniscience.

name: Jambudweep
deity: Jain Tirthankaras, in a complex modelling the Jambudvipa cosmos
significance: A Digambara Jain pilgrimage complex at Hastinapur founded in 1972 by the nun Gyanmati, laid out as a 250-foot circular model of Jambudvipa as described in Jain cosmology, with a 101-foot Mount Sumeru of pink marble at its centre. The model was completed in 1985 and the site is now a major teaching centre for Jain cosmography.
story: Gyanmati is said to have seen the structure of the universe in a vision while meditating in 1965, which she later matched against the cosmographical scriptures and reproduced here.

name: Bade Baba Temple
deity: Rishabhanatha (Adinatha), the first Tirthankara, known here as Bade Baba
significance: The chief Digambara Jain temple of Kundalpur, housing a post-Gupta image of Rishabhanatha venerated as Bade Baba. An eighth-century temple stood here first and was rebuilt in Vikram Samvat 1757 by Bhattaraka Surendrakirti with the help of the Bundela ruler Chhatrasal; the present larger temple was begun in 1997 under Acharya Vidyasagar and received the image in January 2006.
